claims.text: Stripe's Minions system merges over 1,300 pull requests per week that are entirely minion-produced, containing no human-written code but undergoing human review.
Minions' weekly merged PR volume rose from about 1,000 in earlier trials to over 1,300.
By February 2026, Minions were responsible for more than 10% of all code contributions at Stripe.
Minions are allowed at most two rounds of CI, a limit meant to balance speed, cost, and diminishing returns.
If a Minion branch still fails CI after two rounds, it is escalated to a human operator for manual scrutiny.
Stripe's CI selectively runs tests from a battery of over three million tests.
When CI hits a known failure pattern that has an autofix, the autofix is applied automatically; otherwise the failure goes back to the Minion for repair.
Minions run in pre-warmed, standardized AWS EC2 instances called devboxes, which spin up in approximately 10 seconds.
Devboxes are isolated sandboxes, separated from production servers and the internet, which allows Minions to run unattended without risking production stability.
Devboxes mirror a human engineer's environment, with repositories cloned, caches warmed, and background services started ahead of time.
Minions' orchestration mechanism is called 'blueprints': workflows defined in code that intermix deterministic nodes and agentic loops.
Deterministic blueprint nodes handle repeatable tasks such as running linters, pushing changes, and executing specific test suites.
Agentic blueprint nodes handle complex tasks such as implementing features or fixing CI failures, where the agent has tools and freedom to reason.
A local executable runs selected lints on each git push in under five seconds using heuristics, giving the branch a fair chance of passing CI the first time.
The deterministic/agentic split keeps the agent from wasting tokens or CI minutes on trivial tasks like auto-formatting and keeps critical steps consistent.
Before a Minion run, a deterministic orchestrator prehydrates context by scanning the Slack thread for links, pulling Jira tickets, retrieving documentation, and searching code via Sourcegraph.
Stripe's internal MCP server, 'Toolshed', hosts nearly 500 MCP tools spanning internal systems and SaaS platforms.
Each Minion task receives a prefetched subset of about 15 Toolshed tools, chosen by scanning the prompt, to avoid overwhelming the agent.
Agent rules are applied conditionally by subdirectory, so the agent only picks up rules relevant to the code area it is working in.
Every Minion PR is human-reviewed, and reviewing 1,300+ PRs weekly is a noted challenge because AI-written code can be opaque in intent.
Minions perform best on well-defined tasks such as configuration adjustments, dependency upgrades, and minor refactoring.
Engineers can launch multiple Minions in parallel, multiplying their production capacity.
